lesson.title: A Private Hallway Through a Public Building
lesson.summary: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network, most often the public internet, so traffic between two points is shielded from anyone in between as if it were on a private, protected connection.
lesson.body:
The internet is, by design, a network that carries traffic for everyone, and any router along a packet's path could, in principle, inspect or alter that packet. A VPN, or virtual private network, addresses this by building an encrypted tunnel between two points across that untrusted network, so that anyone in between only ever sees unreadable, tamper evident data rather than the original traffic. As covered in the IPsec chapter, one of the most common ways to build this tunnel is by running IPsec in tunnel mode: the original packet is encrypted and wrapped inside a new packet, so intermediate routers only ever see the outer, encrypted envelope rather than the original addressing and payload.

VPNs generally take one of two shapes, and the difference matters for understanding how they're deployed. A remote access VPN connects a single device, like an employee's laptop, into a private network, so that device behaves as though it were physically plugged into that network's internal infrastructure, even from a coffee shop or a home office. A site to site VPN instead connects two entire networks, for example linking a company's headquarters network with a branch office network, so that any device on either side can reach devices on the other side through the encrypted tunnel without each individual device needing its own VPN configuration.

It helps to be precise about what a VPN actually guarantees. It protects the confidentiality and integrity of traffic while that traffic is inside the tunnel, between the two tunnel endpoints. It does not, on its own, protect data once it leaves the tunnel and continues unencrypted across the open internet or arrives at its final destination. That's a common point of confusion: a VPN protects the path, not necessarily everything at either end of that path. It's also why a VPN and TLS often work together rather than substitute for each other. An employee's laptop might connect through a VPN tunnel to reach an internal company server, and still use TLS to protect the specific application connection to that server, the same layered relationship between IPsec and TLS described in the previous chapter.
